name: Anatherum

project_scope.note: Both A. glomeratum and A. virginicum are installed canonical learner species; both species.json records currently carry PASS labels, which are preserved pending any separate scientific review. Familiar aliases are Andropogon glomeratus and Andropogon virginicus. A. glomeratum's current PASS basis lists Williamson County, which is outside the project target-county list; flag for targeted audit rather than changing species-level range decisions here. Do not conflate source-pool A. tenuispatheum with either canonical taxon.

priority: wet-site vs old-field context as secondary support
study_strategy.warning: The familiar Andropogon names are still common in Texas. Search aliases before assuming a record is a separate taxon.

quick_split: Anatherum glomeratum — dense brushlike fluffy crown; many clustered inflorescence units.
Anatherum virginicum — narrower silky racemes, individually more sheath-enclosed; persistent broomlike winter clump.
comparison_lesson.caveat: Both species are canonical and currently PASS under their existing species-level county decisions. The genus comparison needs matched reproductive photographs; A. virginicum currently lacks an images[] gallery.

fast_fill_note: Anatherum glomeratum now has a 3-image FAST-FILL gallery. Synonym-based images are used only because the canonical record explicitly maps Andropogon glomeratus to accepted Anatherum glomeratum.
look_here_first: On a mature flowering stem, follow the upper leaf sheaths to the small paired silky racemes (rames). Is the flowering crown densely packed into a broad brushlike cluster, with many short branches, or is it a narrower, more elongated set of racemes tucked into separate spathe-like sheaths? Then compare the sheath length and how far the rames protrude. Do not key by fall color alone.
shared_genus_traits: Warm-season perennial tufted grasses with leaf sheaths, ligules and narrow blades.
Upper culms bear inflorescence units subtended by spathe-like leafy sheaths.

Each short rame bears paired spikelet positions, typically one fertile sessile spikelet and a reduced or absent pedicellate spikelet; silky hairs on the rame joints and pedicels produce the fluffy appearance.
Andropogon glomeratus and Andropogon virginicus are familiar search aliases for the canonical Anatherum concepts used in this project.

species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-glomeratum: Broad, densely clustered brushlike/cottony terminal mass; shortened upper branches crowded together.
species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-virginicum: Narrower, looser or elongated flowering outline; raceme units distributed along upper branches.

species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-glomeratum: Paired silky rames often reach or protrude from subtending spathes; crowded units form the bushy crown.
species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-virginicum: Short paired or grouped rames mostly partly enclosed by conspicuous flattened spathe-like sheaths.

species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-glomeratum: Rames commonly 1–3 cm, with spathes of roughly similar length in older regional treatments.
species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-virginicum: Rames commonly 1–3 cm; spathes often about 2.5–6 cm. Size overlaps; inspect exposure and architecture.

species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-glomeratum: Frequently low, moist drainage edges, ditches and pond margins.
species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-virginicum: Frequently upland old fields, sandy/disturbed ground; can also occur near bushy bluestem.

species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-glomeratum: Photograph a dense group of paired rames at the upper node and their enclosing spathes.
species_comparison_matrix.anatherum-virginicum: Photograph one separated inflorescence unit with spathe, paired rames and their exposed lengths.

quick_comparison_steps: 1. Start with the whole mature inflorescence: dense rounded brush (glomeratum) versus more elongated and separated units (virginicum).
2. Zoom in on one paired-rame unit and label the spathe, peduncle and two rames.
3. Compare whether rames are protruding or mostly sheath-enclosed; inspect several units because development changes exposure.
4. If uncertain, photograph mature spikelets, sheath attachment and full plant; do not identify by dry-season orange color or habitat alone.
overlap_and_cautions: Both have silky hairs, paired rames and similar spikelet sizes; those shared traits do not separate the species.
Sheath and rame lengths overlap and can change with maturity; overall inflorescence architecture plus rame exposure is stronger than one measurement.
Bushy bluestem can be less conspicuously fluffy before maturity; broomsedge can look crowded on stressed or mowed plants.
Wet versus dry habitat is supporting context only; broomsedge and bushy bluestem can grow together.
A. virginicum is already canonical with species-level PASS status. The older genus-level HOLD text was stale and is superseded by the species record.

The live Master Plant Pool currently lists the two canonical concepts under familiar Andropogon source names; its Anatherum genus row instead counts Anatherum tenuispatheum. Do not manually overwrite Genus Study Index formula columns C:M to mask this source-name mismatch.

Range data integrity: A. glomeratum species.json lists Hays, Travis and Williamson as three target counties, but Williamson is not in PROJECT_RULES.md target zone. Treat its current PASS as a recorded species status requiring targeted Taxonomy + Diagnostic Review; do not use this genus lesson to independently certify a third target county.

local_source_pool_lookalikes.separate: Few open fingerlike turkey-foot racemes, not many paired sheath-enclosed silky rames crowded into a brush.
Silky rames occur singly or in simpler branch arrangements rather than dense upper Anatherum spathe-bracted clusters; confirm spikelet arrangement.
Often conspicuous branching panicles and different raceme/spikelet architecture; inspect rachis and pedicellate spikelets rather than hairiness alone.
